why.correct: The pterion is the small H-shaped area on the side of the skull where the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones meet. It is one of the thinnest parts of the skull.
options: Correct. This is the pterion, where four bones meet over a large artery.
The mastoid process is the knob of the temporal bone behind the ear, lower and farther back.
The zygomatic arch is the bony bar of the cheek below this area.
The coronal suture runs across the top of the head between the frontal and parietal bones; it is one of the seams that ends near here, not the meeting area itself.

why.correct: The zygomatic bone is the cheekbone. It forms the outer wall and part of the floor of the eye socket.
options: The maxilla is the upper jaw, below and toward the midline from the cheekbone.
The nasal bones are the two small bones forming the bridge of the nose.
Correct. The cheekbone is the zygomatic bone.
The temporal bone is a cranial bone on the side of the head around the ear, behind the cheekbone.

why.correct: The foramen magnum is the large hole in the occipital bone. The lower end of the brain passes through it and becomes the spinal cord.
options: The jugular foramen is a smaller opening at the side, between the temporal and occipital bones.
The carotid canal is a small tunnel in the temporal bone that carries the main artery to the front of the brain.
The foramen lacerum is a ragged gap near the tip of the temporal bone's dense ridge, filled with cartilage in life.
Correct. The great central hole in the occipital bone is the foramen magnum.

why.correct: The hypophyseal fossa is the seat of the sella turcica, the saddle-shaped part of the sphenoid bone. It holds the pituitary gland.
options: Correct. This pocket of the sella turcica holds the pituitary gland.
The sphenoid sinus is the air space inside the body of the sphenoid, just below this pocket.
The mandibular fossa is on the underside of the temporal bone, where the jaw hinges, not inside the brain case.
The cribriform plate is the sieve-like part of the ethmoid, farther forward, in the roof of the nose.

why.correct: The maxillary sinus sits in each maxilla, beside the nose and below the eye. It is the largest paranasal sinus.
options: The frontal sinus is in the forehead, above the eyebrows.
The ethmoid air cells are a cluster of small spaces between the eyes.
Correct. The large air space in the cheek is the maxillary sinus.
The sphenoid sinus is deep in the middle of the skull, behind the nose.

why.correct: The anterior fontanelle is the large diamond-shaped soft spot on top of the head where the frontal and parietal bones will meet. It usually closes between about 1 and 2 years of age.
options: The posterior fontanelle is the small triangle at the back of the head, between the parietal and occipital bones.
Correct. The large diamond at the front of the top of the head is the anterior fontanelle.
The sagittal suture is the seam that runs along the midline between the two parietal bones, not the wide membrane-covered area.
An ossification center is the point in the middle of each bone where bone first formed.

why.correct: The mastoid process is the rounded knob of the temporal bone behind the ear. It holds small air cells and anchors muscles of the neck.
options: The styloid process is the thin spike pointing down in front of the mastoid, not the rounded knob.
Correct. The knob behind the ear is the mastoid process.
The occipital condyles are on the underside of the skull beside the foramen magnum.
The condylar process of the mandible is the top of the jaw's upright arm, in front of the ear opening.

why.correct: The vomer is the thin plate forming the lower part of the bony septum of the nose. The perpendicular plate of the ethmoid forms the upper part.
options: Correct. The lower part of the bony wall dividing the nose is the vomer.
The inferior nasal conchae are curled shelves on the side walls of the nose, not the midline wall.
The ethmoid forms the upper part of the bony septum, through its perpendicular plate, not this lower part.
The palatine bones form the back of the bony roof of the mouth, behind and below this area.

why.correct: The lambdoid suture joins the parietal bones to the occipital bone at the back of the skull. With the sagittal suture it forms the shape of the Greek letter lambda.
options: The squamous suture joins the parietal bone to the scale-like upper part of the temporal bone, on the side of the head.
The sagittal suture runs along the midline of the top of the head between the parietal bones.
The coronal suture runs across the top of the head between the frontal and parietal bones.
Correct. The seam between the parietal and occipital bones is the lambdoid suture.

why.correct: The occipital condyles are two rounded knobs beside the foramen magnum. They rest on the topmost vertebra, where the head nods.
options: The mastoid process lies farther out, behind the ear.
Correct. The knobs beside the foramen magnum are the occipital condyles.
The styloid process is a thin spike of the temporal bone, lateral to this area.
The mandibular fossa is a hollow in the temporal bone in front of the ear, where the jaw hinges.

why.correct: The vomer is one of the 14 facial bones. It forms the lower part of the bony septum of the nose.
options: The sphenoid is a cranial bone that stretches across the middle of the skull base.
The ethmoid is a cranial bone, even though much of it sits behind the nose.
Correct. The vomer is a facial bone.
The occipital bone is the cranial bone at the back and base of the brain case.

why.correct: The sagittal suture runs along the midline of the top of the head, in the sagittal plane, joining the two parietal bones.
options: The coronal suture joins the frontal bone to both parietal bones, running across the head from side to side.
Correct. The midline seam between the parietal bones is the sagittal suture.
The lambdoid suture joins the parietal bones to the occipital bone at the back.
The squamous suture joins each parietal bone to the temporal bone below it.

why.correct: Seven bones build each orbit: the frontal, zygomatic, maxilla, lacrimal, ethmoid, sphenoid and palatine. The parietal bones and the vomer are not among them.
options: Yes. The frontal bone forms the roof of the orbit.
No. The parietal bones form the side walls and roof of the brain case, well above and behind the eye.
Yes. The zygomatic bone forms the outer wall and part of the floor.
No. The vomer lies in the midline of the nose, between the two orbits.
Yes. The sphenoid forms the back of the orbit, around the optic canal.
Yes. The small lacrimal bone lies in the inner wall.

why.correct: The blow landed on the pterion, where the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones meet. The bone is thin there, and the artery that enters the skull through the foramen spinosum runs along its inner surface. A crack can tear the artery, and the blood that collects presses on the brain.
options: Correct. The pterion is thin and overlies a large artery.
The foramen magnum is in the base of the skull at the back, far from the side of the head.
The frontal sinus is in the forehead above the eyebrows, not on the side of the head.
The sagittal suture runs along the top midline of the head, far from the side where he was hit, so it is not under this spot.

why.correct: The soft spot on top of the head toward the front is the anterior fontanelle, which stays open until about 1 to 2 years. When an infant loses body water, the volume inside the skull falls a little and the membrane sinks.
options: The posterior fontanelle is at the back of the head and usually closes by 2 to 3 months, and raised pressure makes a soft spot bulge, not sink.
Correct. A sunken anterior fontanelle suggests dehydration.
The location is right, but raised pressure inside the skull makes the fontanelle bulge and feel tense.
The posterior fontanelle is at the back of the head and is usually closed by 9 months.

why.correct: The maxillary sinus sits in the maxilla, in the cheek beside the nose and below the eye. When its lining swells, its opening into the nose closes, mucus builds up and pressure rises.
options: The frontal sinus causes pain above the eyebrow, in the forehead.
The sphenoid sinus is deep in the middle of the skull; its pain is felt deep in the head or behind the eyes.
The ethmoid air cells lie between the eyes, so their pain is felt at the bridge of the nose.
Correct. Cheek pain beside the nose points to the maxillary sinus.

why.correct: Moving back along the floor: the crista galli rises from the ethmoid in the anterior cranial fossa, the sella turcica of the sphenoid sits in the middle cranial fossa, the petrous ridge of each temporal bone marks the back edge of the middle fossa, and the foramen magnum opens in the posterior cranial fossa.
options: The crista galli is in the anterior cranial fossa, the front step.
The sella turcica is in the middle of the skull base, in the middle cranial fossa.
The petrous ridges separate the middle cranial fossa from the posterior one.
The foramen magnum is in the posterior cranial fossa, the deepest step.

why.correct: The bony septum has two parts: the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid above and the vomer below. Septal cartilage completes the wall in front.
options: The inferior nasal conchae are on the side walls of the nose, not in the midline wall.
Correct. The vomer forms the lower part of the bony septum.
The palatine processes of the maxillae form the floor of the nose and the roof of the mouth, below the septum.
The crista galli points up into the brain case from the ethmoid, above the nose.

why.correct: Tears drain from the inner corner of the eye through the groove of the lacrimal bone and down the nasolacrimal canal, which opens into the nose below the inferior nasal concha. They do not enter any sinus.
options: This step is right. Tears flow across the eye to its inner corner.
This step is right. The lacrimal bone (lacrima = tear) holds the groove where drainage begins.
This step is right. The nasolacrimal canal runs between the maxilla and lacrimal bone.
This is the error. The canal opens into the nose under the inferior nasal concha, not into the maxillary sinus.

why.correct: The cribriform plate forms the roof of the nose and the floor under the front of the brain. The nerve fibers for smell pass up through its holes, so a break can tear them, and it can open a path for the fluid around the brain to leak into the nose.
options: A broken zygomatic arch flattens the cheek and can make chewing painful, but it does not open the brain case into the nose.
The sella turcica holds the pituitary gland in the middle of the skull base; it is not where the smell fibers pass.
Correct. A fracture through the cribriform plate explains both findings.
A mastoid fracture is behind the ear; any fluid leak from it comes out of the ear, not the nose, and smell is unaffected.

why.correct: The appendicular skeleton is the limbs plus the bones that attach them to the trunk. The hip bones anchor the legs, so they are appendicular, even though they sit low on the trunk.
options: The hyoid is part of the axial skeleton, in the midline of the neck.
Correct. The hip bones attach the legs to the trunk.
The mandible is a facial bone, part of the skull and so of the axial skeleton.
The breastbone is part of the rib cage, in the axial skeleton.

why.correct: The hyoid hangs in the upper neck by ligaments from the styloid processes and is held by muscles; it does not meet any other bone.
options: The mandible, not the hyoid, is the largest facial bone, and the hyoid is not part of the skull.
The palatine processes of the maxillae and the palatine bones form the bony roof of the mouth.
Correct. The hyoid touches no other bone.
The pituitary gland sits in the hypophyseal fossa of the sphenoid bone.

why.correct: The rounded condylar process at the top back of each ramus of the mandible sits in the mandibular fossa, just in front of the ear.
options: The coronoid process is the flat projection in front, which anchors a chewing muscle.
The angle is the lower back corner of the mandible, below the ear.
Correct. The condylar process fits into the mandibular fossa.
The mental foramen is a hole on the front of the mandible beside the chin.

why.correct: The sella turcica is the saddle-shaped part of the sphenoid bone in the middle of the skull base. Its hypophyseal fossa holds the pituitary gland.
options: The ethmoid lies in front of it and forms the cribriform plate and crista galli.
The temporal bones lie to each side and form the petrous ridges.
The occipital bone lies behind it and holds the foramen magnum.
Correct. The sella turcica is part of the sphenoid.

why.correct: The laminae are the two flat plates that angle in from the pedicles and meet in the midline behind the vertebral foramen, where the spinous process begins.
options: The pedicles are the short stalks that come straight back from the body; the laminae continue from them.
The transverse processes point out to the sides from where each pedicle meets its lamina.
Correct. This flat plate of the arch is a lamina.
The spinous process points backward from where the two laminae meet; it is not the plate itself.

why.correct: The pedicles are the two short, thick stalks that come straight back from the vertebral body and form the sides of the vertebral arch.
options: The laminae are the flat plates behind the pedicles that meet in the midline.
Correct. The short stalk joining the arch to the body is a pedicle.
The vertebral body is the thick front part that bears weight, in front of the arch.
The superior articular processes point upward from the arch and carry the facets that meet the vertebra above.

why.correct: The vertebral foramen is the large hole between the body and the arch. Stacked, the vertebral foramina form the vertebral canal, which holds the spinal cord.
options: The intervertebral foramen is the gap between two neighboring vertebrae, at the side, where a nerve leaves.
Transverse foramina are small holes in the transverse processes of cervical vertebrae only.
Correct. The central hole holding the spinal cord is the vertebral foramen.
Sacral foramina are the paired holes through the sacrum.

why.correct: The dens is the tooth-shaped peg that rises from the body of the axis (C2) into the front of the atlas's ring. The atlas and skull turn around it.
options: Correct. The upward peg of the axis is the dens.
The anterior arch is the front of the atlas's ring, which the dens presses against.
The spinous process points backward from the arch, not up from the body.
The transverse processes point out to the sides.

why.correct: The nucleus pulposus is the soft, gel-like core of the disc, mostly water held by water-binding molecules.
options: The anulus fibrosus is the ring of fibrocartilage around the core, not the core itself.
Correct. The soft center of the disc is the nucleus pulposus.
The vertebral body is bone, above and below the disc.
The ligamentum flavum joins the laminae behind the vertebral canal, not the bodies.

why.correct: The anulus fibrosus is the tough outer ring of the disc: layers of fibrocartilage whose collagen fibers run at alternating angles.
options: The nucleus pulposus is the soft core inside the ring.
The posterior longitudinal ligament runs along the back of the vertebral bodies, not around the disc.
The vertebral foramen is the hole in the vertebra behind the body.
Correct. The fibrous ring is the anulus fibrosus.

why.correct: The sacral promontory is the forward-jutting upper front edge of the first sacral body.
options: The sacral hiatus is the opening at the lower end of the sacral canal, on the back of the sacrum.
The sacral canal runs down inside the sacrum and opens at the top of its back surface, not on its front edge.
Correct. The jutting upper front edge is the sacral promontory.
The coccyx hangs below the sacrum.

why.correct: The nuchal ligament is the thick sheet at the back of the neck, running from C7 up to the back of the skull. It is the neck's version of the supraspinous ligament.
options: The supraspinous ligament joins the tips of the spinous processes from C7 down, below the neck.
Correct. The broad sheet at the nape of the neck is the nuchal ligament.
The anterior longitudinal ligament runs down the front of the vertebral bodies.
The ligamenta flava join the laminae inside the column and cannot be seen from the side like this.

why.correct: The coccyx, the tailbone, is usually four small fused vertebrae hanging below the sacrum.
options: The sacrum is the larger triangular bone just above it.
Correct. The small tail at the bottom is the coccyx.
L5 is the lowest movable vertebra, above the sacrum.
The hip bones lie to each side of the sacrum; they are not part of the column.

why.correct: Costal facets are smooth pits on thoracic vertebrae where the ribs meet the bone: on the sides of the bodies and on the transverse processes of T1 to T10.
options: The superior articular facets are on the upward processes of the arch and meet the vertebra above, not a rib.
Transverse foramina are holes in the transverse processes of cervical vertebrae.
The intervertebral foramen is a gap between two vertebrae, not a smooth pit on one body.
Correct. A rib meets the body at this costal facet.

why.correct: Only cervical vertebrae have transverse foramina. Stacked, they form a channel for the artery that runs up to the back of the brain.
options: Correct. Transverse foramina mark a cervical vertebra.
Thoracic vertebrae have costal facets on their transverse processes, not holes.
Lumbar transverse processes are long and thin, with no holes.
Sacral vertebrae are fused into the sacrum; their holes are the sacral foramina.

why.correct: Lumbar vertebrae carry the weight of the whole trunk, so their bodies are the largest. Their spinous processes are short and hatchet-shaped, and they have neither transverse foramina nor costal facets.
options: Cervical vertebrae have small bodies and holes in their transverse processes.
Thoracic vertebrae have costal facets for ribs and long, downward-sloping spinous processes.
Correct. This is a lumbar vertebra.
Sacral vertebrae are fused into one bone and are not found as single vertebrae in an adult.

why.correct: The atlas is a ring of bone with no body and no spinous process. The occipital condyles of the skull rest in its large upper facets.
options: Yes. The atlas is a ring with a front and back arch and no body.
No. The dens belongs to the axis (C2) and rises into the atlas's ring.
Yes. The atlas has only a small bump where a spinous process would be.
Yes. The skull rocks on these facets when you nod.
No. Bifid spinous processes are found on C2 to C6; the atlas has no spinous process at all.

why.correct: From front to back: the anterior longitudinal ligament covers the front of the bodies; then the vertebral body; the posterior longitudinal ligament on the back of the body; the vertebral canal with the spinal cord; the ligamentum flavum joining the laminae; and the supraspinous ligament on the tips of the spinous processes.
options: The anterior longitudinal ligament lies on the front of the bodies.
The body is the front part of each vertebra.
The posterior longitudinal ligament lies on the back of the bodies, inside the canal.
The canal lies between the body in front and the arch behind.
The ligamentum flavum joins the laminae, which form the back wall of the canal.
The supraspinous ligament joins the tips of the spinous processes, the farthest back.

why.correct: In a herniated disc, the outer rings of the anulus fibrosus tear and the gel of the nucleus pulposus is squeezed out, usually backward and to one side, where it presses on a nerve on its way to an intervertebral foramen.
options: The disc stays anchored to the bodies above and below it; the whole disc does not slide out.
Correct. The nucleus herniates through a tear in the anulus.
The ligamentum flavum is elastic and does not snap with lifting; this would not produce soft disc material on the nerve.
A wedge collapse of a vertebral body is a compression fracture, typical of osteoporosis, and it is bone, not soft disc material.

why.correct: The primary curves are the thoracic and sacrococcygeal curves. They bow backward and are kept from the C-shaped curve of the fetus.
options: The cervical and lumbar curves are the secondary curves, which form after birth.
The thoracic curve is primary, but the lumbar curve is secondary.
The sacrococcygeal curve is primary, but the cervical curve is secondary.
Correct. The thoracic and sacrococcygeal curves are primary.

why.correct: Standing load squeezes water out of the nuclei pulposi, so the discs thin and the person is slightly shorter by evening. The bony vertebral bodies do not change. Lying down overnight lets the discs take water back up.

variables.name: Water content of the nuclei pulposi
variables.why: The weight of the body above squeezes water out of the gel-like nuclei over the day.

variables.name: Height of each intervertebral disc
variables.why: As the nuclei lose water, each disc becomes slightly thinner.

variables.name: The person's total standing height
variables.why: Twenty-three slightly thinner discs add up to a loss of about 1 to 2 cm, regained overnight lying down.

variables.name: Height of each vertebral body
variables.why: The vertebral bodies are bone and do not measurably compress under everyday loads.

why.correct: In osteoporosis, the front of the thoracic vertebral bodies can crush into wedge shapes. Each wedge tilts the column forward, exaggerating the thoracic curve into a hunch (kyphosis) and shortening the trunk.
options: An exaggerated lumbar curve is a swayback (lordosis), which does not round the upper back.
Fused cervical vertebrae would stiffen the neck but would not round the upper back or cost 5 cm.
Correct. Wedge collapse of thoracic bodies produces kyphosis and height loss.
A broken coccyx causes pain on sitting and does not change the curve of the upper back.

why.correct: The vertebral arch is formed by two pedicles that come back from the body and two laminae that meet behind the vertebral foramen.
options: The transverse processes stick out from the arch; they do not form its loop.
Correct. Pedicles and laminae make up the arch.
The articular processes stick up and down from the arch to meet neighboring vertebrae.
Costal facets are smooth pits for ribs on thoracic vertebrae.

why.correct: The sacrum forms from 5 fused sacral vertebrae. The other counts are right: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, and a coccyx of usually 4 (3 to 5) fused vertebrae.
options: This entry is right. There are 7 cervical vertebrae, C1 to C7.
This entry is right. There are 12 thoracic vertebrae, one for each pair of ribs.
This entry is right. There are 5 lumbar vertebrae, L1 to L5.
This is the error. The sacrum forms from 5 fused vertebrae, not 3.
This entry is right. The coccyx usually has 4 fused vertebrae, with 3 to 5 in some people.

why.correct: The ligamentum flavum (flav- = yellow) joins the laminae of neighboring vertebrae. Its elastic fibers give it its yellow color; they stretch when you bend forward and help pull you back upright.
options: The anterior longitudinal ligament is broad, strong dense connective tissue along the front of the bodies.
The posterior longitudinal ligament is a narrow band of dense connective tissue on the back of the bodies.
Correct. The ligamentum flavum is mostly elastic fibers.
The supraspinous ligament is dense connective tissue joining the tips of the spinous processes.

why.correct: Each intervertebral foramen is the gap on either side between two neighboring vertebrae, formed by notches in their pedicles. A nerve leaves the spinal cord through it.
options: The spinal cord runs down the vertebral canal, formed by the stacked vertebral foramina.
Correct. A nerve exits through each intervertebral foramen.
The artery to the back of the brain rises through the transverse foramina of the cervical vertebrae.
The nucleus pulposus stays inside the disc unless it herniates, and then it may press into this gap.

why.correct: Snapping the head back bends the neck backward. The anterior longitudinal ligament runs down the front of the vertebral bodies and resists exactly that movement, so it takes the strain.
options: The supraspinous ligament is on the back of the column; bending backward slackens it.
The ligamenta flava lie behind the canal and are slack, not stretched, when the neck bends backward.
The nuchal ligament at the back of the neck is slackened when the head goes back.
Correct. Backward bending strains the anterior longitudinal ligament.

why.correct: The manubrium is the wide top piece of the sternum. The first ribs and the collarbones attach to it.
options: The body is the long middle piece below the manubrium.
Correct. The wide top piece is the manubrium.
The xiphoid process is the small tip at the bottom.
Costal cartilages are the bars of cartilage at the front ends of the ribs, not part of the sternum.

why.correct: The xiphoid process is the small tip at the bottom of the sternum. No ribs attach to it, and it is cartilage in young people.
options: Correct. The small lower tip is the xiphoid process.
The manubrium is the wide top piece.
The sternal angle is the ridge where the manubrium meets the body, near the top.
The body is the long middle piece above the tip.

why.correct: The sternal angle is the ridge where the manubrium meets the body. The second rib's cartilage attaches at this level.
options: The jugular notch is the dip in the top edge of the manubrium.
The costal margin is the lower edge of the cage, formed by the joined cartilages of the lower ribs.
Correct. The ridge between manubrium and body is the sternal angle.
The clavicular notches are at the upper corners of the manubrium, where the collarbones meet it.

why.correct: The jugular notch, also called the suprasternal notch, is the dip in the top edge of the manubrium, between the inner ends of the collarbones.
options: The sternal angle is a ridge lower down, where the manubrium meets the body.
Correct. The dip at the top of the manubrium is the jugular notch.
The xiphoid process is the tip at the bottom of the sternum.
An intercostal space is a gap between two ribs.

why.correct: The costal cartilages are bars of hyaline cartilage at the front ends of the ribs. They join the ribs to the sternum, directly or through the cartilage above, and let the cage flex.
options: Correct. These bars are the costal cartilages.
The floating ribs are ribs 11 and 12, which have no front attachment.
The costal grooves run along the lower inner edge of each rib, on the inside.
The intercostal spaces are the gaps between neighboring ribs.

why.correct: The head of the rib is its back end. It meets the costal facets of two neighboring vertebral bodies and the disc between them.
options: The tubercle is the small knob farther out that meets the transverse process.
The neck is the narrow part just beyond the head.
Correct. The end that meets the vertebral bodies is the head of the rib.
The angle is the sharp bend beyond the tubercle, where the rib turns forward.

why.correct: The tubercle of the rib is the small knob where the neck meets the body. It meets the costal facet on the transverse process of its own vertebra.
options: The head meets the vertebral bodies, not the transverse process.
The costal facet is the smooth pit on the vertebra, not the knob of the rib that fits into it.
The angle is the sharp bend farther along the rib.
Correct. The knob resting on the transverse process is the tubercle of the rib.

why.correct: The angle of the rib is its point of sharpest bend, a few centimeters beyond the tubercle, where the rib turns forward. It is the rib's weakest point.
options: Correct. The sharp bend is the angle of the rib.
The neck is the short narrow part between the head and the tubercle.
The body is the long curved part in front of the angle, not the bend itself.
The head is the end of the rib that meets the vertebral bodies.

why.correct: Ribs 1 to 7 are true ribs: each one's own costal cartilage reaches the sternum directly.
options: Ribs 6 and 7 also reach the sternum by their own cartilage, so the true ribs run to 7.
Correct. The true ribs are ribs 1 to 7.
Ribs 8 to 10 reach the sternum only through the cartilage of the rib above, so they are false ribs.
Ribs 8 to 12 are the false ribs.

why.correct: The floating ribs, 11 and 12, meet the vertebrae at the back but have no front attachment. Their short cartilages end in the muscles of the abdominal wall.
options: Every rib, floating ribs included, meets the vertebrae at the back.
They do have short cartilage tips; what they lack is a front attachment.
Correct. Floating ribs have no front attachment.
No ribs attach to the xiphoid process.

why.correct: The sternal angle, the ridge where the manubrium meets the body, is level with the cartilage of the second rib. From there she slides sideways onto rib 2 and counts down one rib to rib 3.
options: The jugular notch is the dip at the top of the manubrium, above the level of the first rib, and no rib attaches there.
Correct. The sternal angle marks the second rib.
The xiphoid process has no rib attached, and the seventh rib's cartilage beside it is hard to pick out, so counting from there is unreliable.
The costal margin is formed by the joined cartilages of ribs 7 to 10, so it does not mark a single rib to count from.

why.correct: Compressions go on the lower half of the body of the sternum, in the center of the chest. That pushes the sternum toward the spine over the heart and keeps force off the xiphoid process, which can break and injure the liver.
options: The manubrium lies above most of the heart, and pressing there compresses the heart poorly.
Pushing on the xiphoid can break it and drive it into the liver.
Correct. The lower half of the sternum is the compression point.
The floating ribs are at the sides and back of the lower chest, far from the heart.

why.correct: Each rib has a costal groove along the lower edge of its inner surface, where a nerve, an artery and a vein run. Passing the needle just over the top of the lower rib keeps it away from the groove of the rib above.
options: Costal cartilage is at the front ends of the ribs, not along their edges, and its thickness is not what decides the site.
Correct. The costal groove shelters a nerve and vessels under each rib.
The tubercle is at the back, near the vertebra, not in the space between ribs at the side of the chest.
Sensory endings are not concentrated at the upper edge; the danger is the nerve and vessels running along the lower edge.

why.correct: From back to front: the head meets two vertebral bodies, the neck is the narrow part beyond it, the tubercle meets the transverse process, the angle is the sharp bend, the body curves forward, and the costal cartilage continues it to the front.
options: The head is the back end, against the vertebral bodies.
The neck comes right after the head.
The tubercle sits where the neck meets the rest of the rib.
The angle is the sharp bend just beyond the tubercle.
The body curves forward around the side of the chest.
The costal cartilage continues the rib at its front end.

why.correct: The false ribs are ribs 8 to 12: their own cartilage does not reach the sternum. Ribs 11 and 12, the floating ribs, are false ribs too.
options: No. Rib 3 is a true rib: its own cartilage reaches the sternum.
No. Rib 7 is the last true rib.
Yes. Rib 8's cartilage joins the cartilage of rib 7.
Yes. Rib 10's cartilage joins the cartilage of rib 9.
Yes. Rib 12 is a floating rib, which is a kind of false rib.

why.correct: A rib's head meets the body of its own vertebra and the one above, so rib 5 meets T4 and T5. Its tubercle meets its own vertebra's transverse process, T5.
options: T3 is two levels above; rib 4 meets T3 and T4.
Correct. Rib 5 meets the bodies of T4 and T5.
T6 is below; rib 6 meets T5 and T6.
T7 is too far down; rib 7 meets T6 and T7.

why.correct: Rib 8 is a false rib. Its costal cartilage joins the cartilage of rib 7, so it reaches the sternum only indirectly.
options: This statement is right. A rib's head meets its own vertebra and the one above.
This statement is right. The tubercle meets its own vertebra's transverse process.
This statement is right. The body of every rib curves forward around the chest.
This is the error. Rib 8's cartilage joins the cartilage of rib 7.

why.correct: When several neighboring ribs each break in two places, a section of the chest wall is cut loose from the cage: a flail chest. When she breathes in, the rest of the cage widens and pressure inside the chest falls, so the loose section is pulled inward instead of moving out.
options: Ribs 4 to 7 are true ribs, not floating ribs, and a loose floating rib would not produce this pattern.
The xiphoid process has no ribs attached, so it cannot pull ribs inward.
Calcified cartilage stiffens the chest evenly; it does not make one patch move the wrong way.
Correct. The loose segment is cut off from the cage and moves the opposite way to the rest of the chest.

why.correct: The xiphoid process, the small lower tip, has no ribs attached. Rib 1 attaches to the manubrium, rib 2 at the sternal angle, and ribs 3 to 7 to the body.
options: The first ribs attach to the manubrium.
The cartilages of ribs 2 to 7 attach along the body.
Correct. No ribs attach to the xiphoid process.
The second rib's cartilage attaches right at the sternal angle.

why.correct: The costal cartilages are hyaline cartilage, which bends and springs back. They link the ribs to the sternum without rigid bone, so the cage can flex and the ribs can swing up and out.
options: Sutures are seams between skull bones; the ribs are not joined to each other by sutures.
Ribs are not hollow; like other bones they have spongy bone inside compact bone.
The floating ribs are free at the front, but they are only two pairs and do not make the whole cage flexible.
Correct. The costal cartilages, made of hyaline cartilage, give the cage its flexibility.

why.correct: The acromion is the flat end of the scapula's spine. It forms the bony tip of the shoulder and meets the clavicle.
options: The coracoid process is the hook that points forward under the clavicle.
Correct. The flat projection at the tip of the shoulder is the acromion.
The glenoid cavity is the shallow socket on the outer corner, where the humerus fits.
The spine is the ridge across the back of the scapula; the acromion is its end.

why.correct: The coracoid process is the beak-like hook that points forward under the clavicle. Muscles of the chest and arm anchor to it.
options: The acromion is the flat tip of the shoulder at the end of the spine.
The glenoid cavity is the socket for the humerus, below and lateral to the hook.
Correct. The forward-pointing hook is the coracoid process.
The superior angle is the upper corner of the triangle, on the medial side.

why.correct: The glenoid cavity is the shallow oval socket on the lateral corner of the scapula. The head of the humerus fits into it.
options: Correct. The socket for the head of the humerus is the glenoid cavity.
The subscapular fossa is the broad hollow on the front surface facing the ribs.
The acromion is the flat tip of the shoulder above the socket.
The infraspinous fossa is the hollow below the spine on the back.

why.correct: The supraspinous fossa is the hollow on the back of the scapula above the spine (supra- = above).
options: The infraspinous fossa is the larger hollow below the spine.
The subscapular fossa is on the front surface, facing the ribs.
Correct. The hollow above the spine is the supraspinous fossa.
The olecranon fossa is on the back of the lower humerus, not the scapula.

why.correct: The greater tubercle is the large bump on the lateral side of the top of the humerus. Muscles that steady the shoulder anchor to it.
options: The lesser tubercle is the smaller bump on the front, across the groove.
Correct. The large lateral bump is the greater tubercle.
The deltoid tuberosity is a rough patch halfway down the shaft.
The head is the smooth half-ball that fits into the glenoid cavity.

why.correct: The surgical neck is the narrowing of the shaft just below the tubercles. It is a common fracture site, especially in older adults.
options: The anatomical neck is the groove right at the edge of the head, above the tubercles.
The intertubercular groove is the channel between the tubercles, running up and down.
The deltoid tuberosity is farther down, halfway along the lateral shaft.
Correct. The narrowing below the tubercles is the surgical neck.

why.correct: The capitulum is the rounded knob on the lateral side of the lower humerus. The head of the radius meets it.
options: The trochlea is the spool on the medial side, which the ulna wraps around.
The medial epicondyle is the knob that sticks out on the inner side of the elbow, not the rounded surface in front.
Correct. The rounded lateral knob is the capitulum.
The head of the radius is on the forearm bone below, not part of the humerus.

why.correct: The olecranon fossa is the deep hollow on the back of the lower humerus. The olecranon of the ulna slots into it when the elbow straightens.
options: Correct. The deep hollow on the back is the olecranon fossa.
The coronoid fossa is the smaller hollow on the front of the humerus.
The radial fossa is a small hollow on the front, above the capitulum.
The trochlear notch is on the ulna, not the humerus.

why.correct: The radial tuberosity is the rough bump just below the head of the radius, where the tendon of the main muscle on the front of the arm anchors.
options: The head of the radius is the disc at the very top, above this bump.
Correct. The bump below the head of the radius is the radial tuberosity.
The coronoid process belongs to the ulna and juts forward from its notch.
The styloid process of the radius is at the wrist end.

why.correct: The trochlear notch is the large C-shaped notch at the top of the ulna. It wraps around the trochlea of the humerus.
options: The olecranon is the hooked point above and behind the notch.
The coronoid process is the lower lip of the notch, not the notch itself.
The radial tuberosity is on the radius.
Correct. The C-shaped notch is the trochlear notch.

why.correct: The scaphoid (scaph- = boat) is the lateral bone of the proximal row, on the thumb side. It meets the radius.
options: The trapezium is in the distal row, at the base of the thumb.
The lunate is next to the scaphoid, toward the little finger.
Correct. The boat-shaped bone on the thumb side of the proximal row is the scaphoid.
The capitate is the large central bone of the distal row.

why.correct: The hamate is the medial bone of the distal row, on the little-finger side. It has a hook on its palm side (ham- = hook).
options: The pisiform is the small pea-shaped bone in the proximal row.
Correct. The medial bone of the distal row is the hamate.
The triquetrum is in the proximal row, under the pisiform.
The trapezoid is in the distal row on the thumb side, next to the trapezium.

why.correct: The flexor retinaculum is the tough band of dense connective tissue stretched across the palm side of the carpals. It turns their U-shaped trough into the carpal tunnel.
options: Correct. The band across the top is the flexor retinaculum.
The hamate is one of the carpals forming the wall of the tunnel.
The carpal tunnel is the passage itself, not the band that roofs it.
The tendons pass through the tunnel under the band.

why.correct: The clavicle meets the manubrium of the sternum at one end and the acromion of the scapula at the other. The scapula itself is held to the trunk only by muscles.
options: The scapula does not meet the vertebral column or the ribs; muscles hold it against the back of the rib cage.
The humerus meets the scapula, not the axial skeleton.
Correct. The clavicle is the only bony link.
The first rib is part of the axial skeleton itself, not a link to the limb.

why.correct: The surgical neck is the narrowing of the shaft just below the greater and lesser tubercles, and it is where the upper humerus most often breaks in older adults.
options: The anatomical neck is above the tubercles, at the edge of the head, and it rarely breaks.
The deltoid tuberosity is halfway down the shaft.
Correct. A break below the tubercles is at the surgical neck.
The lateral epicondyle is at the lower end of the humerus, at the elbow.

why.correct: The tender hollow at the base of the thumb lies over the scaphoid, the carpal broken most often in this kind of fall. A scaphoid crack may not show on the first X-ray. Blood vessels enter the scaphoid mainly at its far end, so a break can starve the near piece, which may die and fail to heal. Splinting protects it until a later image settles the question.
options: Correct. A missed scaphoid fracture risks losing the blood supply to part of the bone.
The pisiform is on the little-finger side of the palm, not the thumb side, and it does not slip out of its tendon.
The scaphoid, not the lunate, is the carpal broken most often.
The fifth metacarpal is at the little-finger side, usually broken by punching, not tender at the base of the thumb.

why.correct: This is carpal tunnel syndrome. The carpals form the floor and walls of the carpal tunnel, and the flexor retinaculum stretches across the top as its roof. When the tendons in the tunnel swell, the tight band cannot give, so the nerve is squeezed.
options: Correct. The flexor retinaculum is the roof of the carpal tunnel.
The hamate is one of the carpals in the wall of the tunnel, not its roof.
The trochlear notch is on the ulna at the elbow.
The head of the ulna is at the wrist but on the little-finger side, outside the tunnel.

why.correct: The ulna carries the olecranon, the trochlear notch and the coronoid process at its upper end, and a small head and styloid process at the wrist.
options: Yes. The olecranon is the point of the elbow, on the ulna.
No. The radial tuberosity is on the radius, below its head.
Yes. The trochlear notch of the ulna wraps around the trochlea.
No. The capitulum is on the lower humerus.
Yes. The coronoid process of the ulna is the lower lip of its notch.

why.correct: From the thumb side: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform, the first four words of "Some Lovers Try Positions".
options: The scaphoid is on the thumb side and meets the radius.
The lunate sits beside the scaphoid and also meets the radius.
The triquetrum is next, toward the little finger.
The pisiform sits on the palm side of the triquetrum, farthest medial.

why.correct: The capitulum is the rounded knob on the lateral side of the lower humerus, and the disc-shaped head of the radius meets it.
options: The olecranon fossa receives the olecranon of the ulna when the elbow straightens.
Correct. The head of the radius meets the capitulum.
The medial epicondyle is a knob on the inner side for muscle attachment; no forearm bone meets it.
The greater tubercle is at the top of the humerus, at the shoulder.

why.correct: In anatomical position, with the palm forward, the ulna is on the medial, little-finger side, and the radius is on the lateral, thumb side.
options: This is the error. The radius is on the thumb side; the ulna is on the little-finger side.
This statement is right. The ulna's big end, with the olecranon and trochlear notch, is at the elbow.
This statement is right. The radius's wide end carries the wrist.
This statement is right. The radius swings across the front of the ulna when the palm turns down.

why.correct: The thumb has 2 phalanges and each of the four fingers has 3, for 2 + 12 = 14.
options: Ten would be two per digit, but only the thumb has two.
Fifteen would be three per digit, but the thumb has only two.
Correct. There are 14 phalanges in each hand.
Five is the number of metacarpals, not phalanges.

why.correct: The "funny bone" is not a bone. A nerve runs in a groove on the back of the medial epicondyle of the humerus with only skin over it, and a knock squeezes it against the bone, sending tingling along its path to the little finger.
options: Correct. He hit a nerve lying against the medial epicondyle.
The olecranon is the point of the elbow; bruising it hurts locally but does not send tingling to the little finger.
The radial tuberosity is on the front of the forearm below the elbow, deep under muscle.
The capitulum is on the lateral side at the front of the elbow, covered by other structures.

why.correct: The acetabulum is the deep cup-shaped socket on the outer side of the hip bone, where the ilium, ischium and pubis meet. The head of the femur fits into it.
options: The obturator foramen is the large hole below the socket, not the socket itself.
The iliac fossa is the broad shallow hollow on the inner surface of the ilium.
The greater sciatic notch is a deep notch on the back edge of the hip bone.
Correct. The deep socket is the acetabulum.

why.correct: The iliac crest is the curved upper edge of the ilium, the part you feel when you put your hands on your hips.
options: Correct. The long curved upper edge is the iliac crest.
The pelvic brim is the rim around the inside of the pelvis, lower down, not the upper edge.
The ischial spine is a pointed projection on the back of the ischium.
The anterior superior iliac spine is only the front end point of the crest, not the whole edge.

why.correct: The anterior superior iliac spine is the front end of the iliac crest, a bony point you can feel at the front of your hip.
options: The posterior superior iliac spine is at the back end of the crest.
The ischial spine is on the ischium, low on the back of the hip bone.
Correct. The front end of the crest is the anterior superior iliac spine.
The greater trochanter is on the femur, below the hip bone.

why.correct: The ischial tuberosity is the thick, rough base of the ischium. You sit on your two ischial tuberosities.
options: The ischial spine is the pointed projection higher up on the back of the ischium.
The pubic symphysis is at the front midline, where the two pubic bones meet.
The obturator foramen is the large hole above and in front of this area.
Correct. The thick base of the ischium is the ischial tuberosity.

why.correct: The obturator foramen is the large hole surrounded by the pubis and ischium, below the acetabulum. A membrane closes almost all of it.
options: The acetabulum is the socket above the hole.
The greater sciatic notch is on the back edge of the hip bone, not a closed hole.
Correct. The large hole below the socket is the obturator foramen.
The pelvic inlet is the upper opening of the whole lesser pelvis, not a hole in one hip bone.

why.correct: The pubic symphysis is where the two pubic bones meet at the front midline, joined by a pad of fibrocartilage.
options: Correct. The front midline meeting point is the pubic symphysis.
The sacral promontory is at the back, the upper front edge of the sacrum.
The coccyx is at the back, below the sacrum.
The pelvic brim is the rim around the inside of the pelvis, which passes the top of this point but is not the point itself.

why.correct: The greater trochanter is the large bump on the lateral side where the neck of the femur meets the shaft. It is the bony point you feel on the side of your hip.
options: The lesser trochanter is the smaller bump lower down on the back and inner side.
The head is the smooth ball that fits into the acetabulum.
Correct. The large lateral bump at the top of the shaft is the greater trochanter.
The lateral epicondyle is at the knee end of the femur.

why.correct: The linea aspera is the rough line running down the back of the femur's shaft, where many thigh muscles anchor.
options: Correct. The rough line down the back of the shaft is the linea aspera.
The intertrochanteric crest runs between the trochanters at the top, not down the shaft.
The neck joins the head to the shaft at the top of the bone.
The anterior border is the sharp front edge of the tibia, the shin.

why.correct: The tibial tuberosity is the bump on the front of the tibia just below the knee, where the tendon running down from the patella anchors.
options: The medial condyle is the broad upper surface on the inner side, above this bump.
The head of the fibula is on the outer side, below the lateral condyle of the tibia.
Correct. The bump below the knee is the tibial tuberosity.
The medial malleolus is at the ankle end of the tibia.

why.correct: The lateral malleolus is the lower end of the fibula, the bump on the outer side of the ankle. It sits lower than the medial malleolus.
options: Correct. The outer ankle bump is the lateral malleolus.
The medial malleolus is on the tibia, at the inner ankle.
The calcaneus is the heel bone, below and behind the ankle.
The head of the fibula is at the top of the fibula, below the knee.

why.correct: The calcaneus is the heel bone, the largest tarsal, lying below the talus. The thick tendon of the calf muscles anchors to its back.
options: The talus sits on top of the calcaneus and meets the tibia.
The cuboid is in front of the calcaneus, on the outer side of the foot.
The navicular is in front of the talus, on the inner side of the foot.
Correct. The heel bone is the calcaneus.

why.correct: The navicular (little boat) sits in front of the talus on the inner side of the foot, behind the three cuneiforms.
options: Correct. The bone in front of the talus on the inner side is the navicular.
The cuboid is on the outer side of the foot, in front of the calcaneus.
The medial cuneiform is one step farther forward, in front of the navicular.
The talus is behind the navicular, on top of the calcaneus.

why.correct: The subpubic angle is the angle at the top of the pubic arch, below the pubic symphysis. It is wide in the female pelvis and narrow in the male pelvis.
options: Correct. The angle below the pubic symphysis is the subpubic angle.
The pelvic inlet is the upper opening outlined by the pelvic brim.
The pelvic brim is the outlined rim of the inlet.
The sacral promontory is at the back of the inlet.

why.correct: The sacrotuberous ligament runs from the side of the sacrum to the ischial tuberosity. The shorter sacrospinous ligament runs to the ischial spine.
options: The sacrospinous ligament runs to the ischial spine, higher and shorter.
The posterior longitudinal ligament runs inside the vertebral canal, along the back of the vertebral bodies.
The supraspinous ligament joins the tips of the spinous processes of the vertebrae.
Correct. The ligament to the ischial tuberosity is the sacrotuberous ligament.

why.correct: The three parts of the hip bone meet and fuse in the acetabulum, the socket for the femoral head.
options: At the pubic symphysis, the right and left pubic bones meet each other; the ilium does not reach it.
The obturator foramen is surrounded by the pubis and ischium only.
Correct. All three meet in the acetabulum.
The greater sciatic notch is formed mostly by the ilium.

why.correct: A light build, a shallow lesser pelvis, a round inlet and a subpubic angle near 90 degrees or more are all features of the average female pelvis. The male pelvis is heavier and deeper, with a heart-shaped inlet and a subpubic angle of about 50 to 60 degrees.
options: A male pelvis is usually heavier and deeper, with a heart-shaped inlet and a narrow subpubic angle of about 50 to 60 degrees.
Correct. These features together point to a female pelvis.
Individual pelves overlap, but the pelvis is one of the most reliable parts of the skeleton for judging sex, especially when several features agree, as they do here.

why.correct: The femoral neck joins the head to the shaft at an angle, and it is the femur's weak point. In older adults a fall on the side of the hip often breaks it; this is what most people call a broken hip.
options: The linea aspera runs down the back of the shaft, below the trochanters.
Correct. The break is through the femoral neck.
The lateral condyle is at the knee end of the femur.
The lesser trochanter is below the neck, and a break of it alone would not fit a break between the head and the greater trochanter.

why.correct: On average the female pelvis has a wider subpubic angle, a shallower lesser pelvis, a round inlet, ischial spines farther apart and a shorter, wider, less curved sacrum.
options: Yes. The female subpubic angle is about 80 to 90 degrees or more.
No. A heart-shaped inlet is typical of the male pelvis; the female inlet is round or oval.
Yes. The female lesser pelvis is shallower.
No. In the female pelvis the ischial spines are farther apart.
Yes. The female sacrum is shorter, wider and less curved.

why.correct: The trunk's weight passes from the sacrum into the ilium, around to the acetabulum, into the head of the femur, down the femur to the tibia, and from the tibia to the talus, which spreads it to the rest of the foot.
options: The sacrum receives the weight of the trunk from the vertebral column.
The ilium takes the load from the sacrum.
The acetabulum is the socket where the load leaves the hip bone.
The head of the femur sits in the acetabulum.
The femur rests on the tibia, which carries almost all the weight in the leg.
The talus is the only foot bone the tibia rests on.

why.correct: The medial malleolus is the lower end of the tibia, the bump on the inner ankle. The lateral malleolus is the lower end of the fibula.
options: Correct. The medial malleolus belongs to the tibia.
The talus is the foot bone gripped between the two malleoli.
The femur ends at the knee, far above the ankle.
The calcaneus is the heel bone, below the talus.

why.correct: The cuboid lies on the outer (lateral) side of the foot, in front of the calcaneus. The navicular is the tarsal on the inner side, in front of the talus.
options: This statement is right. The tibia rests only on the talus.
This statement is right. The calcaneus is the heel bone.
This is the error. The cuboid is on the outer side of the foot.
This statement is right. The three cuneiforms sit in a row in front of the navicular.

why.correct: The patella forms inside the tendon of the large muscle group on the front of the thigh, which makes it a sesamoid bone, and it is the largest one.
options: The pisiform is a sesamoid bone in the wrist, but it is pea-sized.
Correct. The patella is the largest sesamoid bone.
The calcaneus is the largest tarsal, but it is not a sesamoid bone.
The talus is a tarsal bone, not a sesamoid bone.

why.correct: The second and third metatarsals are long and thin and take repeated load in running. Mounting mileage can crack them without a single injury: a stress fracture. Pain on the top of the foot, in line with the second toe and just back from it, points to the second metatarsal.
options: The talus is at the ankle, under the tibia, not in the middle of the foot.
Correct. The second metatarsal is the classic site of a runner's stress fracture.
The navicular is on the inner side of the foot, behind the cuneiforms.
The proximal phalanx is in the toe itself, beyond the ball of the foot.

why.correct: The plantar aponeurosis is a thick sheet of dense connective tissue on the sole, running from the calcaneus to the toes. When it is strained where it anchors to the calcaneus, heel pain is worst with the first steps after rest: plantar fasciitis.
options: Correct. The plantar aponeurosis anchors to the calcaneus under the heel.
The lateral malleolus is at the outer ankle, not under the heel.
The head of the fibula is below the knee.
The pubic symphysis is at the front of the pelvis.

why.correct: The fibula does not reach the femur. Its head sits below the lateral condyle of the tibia, on the outer side, below the knee.
options: The femur's condyles form the top of the knee.
The tibia's condyles carry the femur at the knee.
The patella glides on the front of the femur at the knee.
Correct. The fibula is not part of the knee.
